newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA GROUPS FIGHT FOR SLICE OF PETROL PRICE PIE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA GROUPS FIGHT FOR SLICE OF PETROL PRICE PIE.

text.p: At a time of rising oil prices and a weak rand, the last thing the South Africa government needs is growing pressure from several quarters for a bigger slice of the petrol price.

But that is exactly what confronts it at the end of 1996 with at least three pleas for a portion of the petrol price that could collectively increase prices by as much as 11.5 cents over and above monthly price adjustments.

The oil industry is due three cents a litre to top up its wholesale margin, Transport Minister Mac Maharaj wants six to seven cents a litre for a dedicated road fund and the state motor accident fund wants the 1.5 cents it was promised this year - and even more if possible to wipe out a growing deficit.
Newly appointed Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna and a special Cabinet committee are grappling with all of these issues, but no one expects any quick answers.

The basic price of petrol only makes up about 30 percent of pump prices, with the rest being divided between the government, industry mark-ups, the Multilateral Motor Vehicle Accidents Fund (MMF), transport costs and the Equalisation Fund used to help subidise synthetic oil producer, Sasol Ltd .

Apportioning an extra bite of the "petrol pie" to any one of these competing interests means increasing the petrol price, unless this can be fudged when there is a monthly downward adjustment of the petrol price according to a complicated formula based on international oil prices and the rand exchange rate.
At the moment, however, the pressure on the petrol price is upwards and adding anything else on top of that would be hugely unpopular, especially with the volatile minibus taxi industry.

Econometrix director Tony Twine said it would be difficult politically to grant any of the requests for a bigger slice of the oil price "while we are staring down the barrel of an oil price of $25" and an steadily depreciating rand.
One solution might be to grant a portion of the requests out of the 5.4 cents a litre levy building up in the Equalisation Fund because Sasol does not need subsidies at current high oil prices.
"That will be a short term expedience but it would not solve the whole problem," Twine said.

South African Petroleum Industry Association director Colin McClelland agreed that this could be an option. But he warned that if the oil price fell, the full benefits would not be felt by the public as the slice going to the Equalisation Fund would have to be restored to pay Sasol's subsidy.
"One way out of this is to deregulate, but that has its complications too," McClelland said.

Unions are opposed to deregulation because it could lead to job losses if service stations switched to self-service and large supermarkets such as Pick 'n Pay Stores Ltd opened cut-price outlets, taking business away from black owned service stations.
Maharaj's proposed road fund levy would be the largest new demand on the petrol price, but both Twine and McClelland said that finding other ways to fund the maintenance of roads would not be easy.
Twine said that turning all major roads into toll roads would take time and would also make government unpopular with a lot of voters.
